objective: By the end of this lesson you can find and explain the airplane's certificates and logbook entries, decide if the airplane is airworthy, and handle inoperative equipment the legal way.
why: The pilot in command is the one who decides if the airplane is safe to fly. A missed inspection, an open AD or a broken light you ignore can make a flight illegal or unsafe.

prereading.what: Aircraft documents, inspections, MEL and inoperative equipment, preventive maintenance, special flight permits, ADs.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 9, 9-6 to 9-13

prereading.what: How a pilot checks logbooks and documents before the visual preflight.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-4

prereading.what: Day and night VFR equipment lists.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.205

prereading.what: Inoperative instruments and equipment, with and without an MEL.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.213

prereading.label: AC 91-67A, Ch 4

prereading.label: 14 CFR 21.197 and 21.199

warmup: You arrive for a flight and the left wing position light will not come on. It is noon. Can you go? Would your answer change if you planned to land after sunset?

key_terms.def: The aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation (14 CFR 3.5(a), as quoted in AFH 2-1).
Inspection every aircraft needs within the preceding 12 calendar months.
Extra inspection for aircraft carrying people for hire, or used for flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides.
12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year.
A legally enforceable FAA rule that fixes an unsafe condition in an aircraft, engine, propeller or appliance.
A special airworthiness certificate that lets an aircraft that does not meet airworthiness rules, but is safe, make a specific flight (for example, to a repair shop).
Simple or minor preservation work and replacing small standard parts, limited to the list in 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c).
Minimum Equipment List: an FAA-approved list, with a Letter of Authorization, that lets a specific aircraft fly with certain items inoperative.
Kinds of Operations Equipment List: shows the equipment required for each kind of flight operation (named in 14 CFR 91.213(d)).
A label placed on a broken instrument or its cockpit control so no one relies on it.

body.p: Airworthy means the airplane matches its type design and is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]]. No one may fly a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(a)]].

head: Owner / operator
Pilot in command (PIC)
rows: Primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy, including ADs [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]
Decides if the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]
Gets required inspections done and has defects repaired between inspections [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]]
Must end the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]
Makes sure mechanics make logbook entries approving return to service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(b)]]
Checks logbooks or an airworthiness summary before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]
Keeps airworthiness and registration certificates in the aircraft; notifies the FAA Registry of address change, sale or export [[1:243|PHAK 9-13]]
Follows the AFM/POH limitations, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]

body.p: After any maintenance, no one may fly the aircraft until a person authorized under 14 CFR 43.7 approves it for return to service and the logbook entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

callout.text: If maintenance may have changed how the airplane flies, no passengers may ride until a pilot with at least a private pilot certificate test-flies it and logs the flight in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]].

check.q: The owner is responsible for maintenance. So is the PIC off the hook?
check.a: No. The PIC must still determine the aircraft is in condition for safe flight and stop the flight if it becomes unairworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

chunks.title: Documents on board: where and how long they last

body.p: Two certificates must be in the airplane: a current airworthiness certificate and an effective U.S. registration certificate [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]]. The airworthiness certificate must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so passengers or crew can read it [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].

bullets: Registration: must be carried in the aircraft at all times [[1:236|PHAK 9-6]].
Registration expires seven years after the last day of the month it was issued. Renew with AC Form 8050-1B and the fee during the six months before it expires [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)-(b)]].

It is no longer valid if the aircraft is registered in a foreign country, the owner asks to cancel it, the aircraft is destroyed or scrapped, ownership is transferred, or the holder loses U.S. citizenship [[1:236|PHAK 9-6]].

New owner: carry the second (pink) copy of the registration application (AC Form 8050-1) as temporary authority, for operation inside the United States only. It lasts until you receive the certificate or the FAA denies the application [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)(1)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]]. It cannot be used if 12 months have passed since the first application after the ownership transfer [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)(2)]].

Airworthiness certificate: stays in effect as long as maintenance and alterations follow Parts 21, 43 and 91 and the aircraft is registered in the U.S. [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. It stays with the aircraft unless sold to a foreign buyer [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]].

body.p: Other items the pilot checks are on board or attached [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]:

bullets: Radio station license, for flights outside the U.S. or airplanes over 12,500 pounds (FCC rule)
Operating limitations: FAA-approved AFM/POH, placards, instrument markings, or a mix [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]]
Current weight and balance data
Compass correction card, if required
External data plate (14 CFR 45.11)

callout.text: ARROW (study aid built from the AFH list): Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Radio license (if needed), Operating limitations, Weight and balance.
Logbooks are normally NOT kept in the airplane [[24:39|AFH 2-2]]. Know where your school keeps them.

check.q: You just bought an airplane and have only the pink copy of the registration application. Can you fly to Canada?
check.a: No. The pink copy is temporary authority only for operation within the United States [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)(1)]] [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]].

head: Standard (FAA Form 8100-2)
Special (FAA Form 8130-7)
rows: Issued for
Normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter, transport categories and manned free balloons [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]]
Experimental, restricted, limited, provisional, light-sport (LSA); also special flight permits [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]
Look
See figure above (FAA Form 8100-2)
LSA receive a pink special certificate [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]
Equipment rule
91.205 equipment list applies [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]]
Its own operating limitations apply
Annual / 100-hour (91.409)
Required
Not required for special flight permit, experimental, LSA or provisional; other rules apply [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)(1)]]

body.p: Special certificates come with limits. Two common ones:

bullets: Experimental: fly only for the purpose it was issued; tell each person carried it is experimental; VFR day only unless authorized; tell ATC it is experimental when using ATC services [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319]].

Light-sport: no compensation or hire except towing, flight training/checking/testing, or listed aerial work; a condition inspection every 12 calendar months; comply with all ADs [[60:518|14 CFR 91.327]].

callout.text: Buying an aircraft that is not Standard? The PHAK suggests calling the local FSDO to learn its airworthiness rules and limits [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

check.q: Your friend's experimental airplane: what must he tell you before you ride along?
check.a: That the aircraft is experimental [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319(d)(1)]].

head: Inspection
When
Rule
rows: Annual
Within the preceding 12 calendar months, for every aircraft (except those listed in 91.409(c), such as experimental, LSA, or a progressive inspection program)
100-hour
Within the preceding 100 hours time in service if carrying anyone (not crew) for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides
ELT inspection
Within 12 calendar months after the last inspection
ELT battery
Replace (or recharge) after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of useful life has expired
Transponder
Tested within the preceding 24 calendar months
Altimeter / static system
Within the preceding 24 calendar months, for IFR in controlled airspace
Airworthiness Directives
As each AD requires (one time or recurring)

callout.text: 12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the LAST day of that month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Annual signed off March 3 = good through March 31 next year.

bullets: 100-hour limit can be exceeded by not more than 10 hours to reach a place where the inspection can be done. That extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

An annual can take the place of a 100-hour [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. A 100-hour cannot count as an annual unless done by someone authorized to do annuals and logged as an annual [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].
Who: annual by an A&P with an Inspection Authorization (IA), the manufacturer, or a rated repair station; 100-hour by an A&P, repair station or manufacturer [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

check.q: A rental airplane (used for instruction for hire) reached 100 hours since its last inspection while away from home. How far over can it go?
check.a: Not more than 10 hours, only to reach a place where the inspection can be done; those hours count toward the next 100 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

body.p: Each airplane has airframe and engine logbooks, and sometimes propeller and appliance logbooks [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].
An inspection entry must show [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]]:

bullets: Type of inspection and a short description of its extent
Date and aircraft total time in service
Signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving (or not approving) return to service
A statement like: 'I certify that this aircraft has been inspected in accordance with (type) inspection and was determined to be in airworthy condition.'

body.p: If the inspector finds problems, the entry instead says the aircraft was inspected and a dated list of discrepancies and unairworthy items was given to the owner, and the owner gets that signed and dated list [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)(5)]] [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].

head: Owner must keep
How long
rows: Maintenance, preventive maintenance, alteration and inspection records (what was done, date, signature and certificate number)
Until the work is repeated or superseded, or 1 year after the work [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(1)]]
Total time; life-limited parts status; time since overhaul; current inspection status; AD status (method, AD number, revision date, next due if recurring); Form 337s for major alterations
Kept and transferred with the aircraft when sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(2)]]
List of defects from an inspection
Until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]]

check.q: What four things must the logbook show about AD status?
check.a: The method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and, if recurring, the time and date of the next required action [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

body.p: ADs are legally enforceable rules for aircraft, engines, propellers and appliances [[60:125|14 CFR 39.3]]. The FAA issues one when an unsafe condition exists and is likely in other products of the same type design [[60:125|14 CFR 39.5]].

bullets: Flying with an AD not complied with is a violation, every time you operate [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7, 39.9]].
An AD applies even if the product was modified in that area [[60:125|14 CFR 39.15]].
Two kinds: emergency ADs (comply before further flight) and less urgent ADs (comply within a set time) [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
Recurring ADs repeat, for example an inspection every 50 hours. You may not overfly the hour limit unless the AD itself allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
If an AD conflicts with the manufacturer's service document, follow the AD [[60:126|14 CFR 39.27]].
The owner/operator makes sure ADs are complied with [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]] [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

callout.text: Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins (SAIBs) are not covered in the FAA resources used for this lesson. Your CFI will cover them (see gaps).

check.q: An AD needs an inspection every 50 hours. The airplane is at 50.5 hours since the last one. Can you fly it home first?
check.a: No, not unless the AD itself allows it; there is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. A special flight permit may be possible [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]].

body.p: A special flight permit is a special airworthiness certificate. It lets an aircraft that does not meet airworthiness rules, but is safe for the flight, make a specific flight [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

bullets: Fly to a base for repairs, alterations or maintenance, or to a point of storage
Deliver or export the aircraft
Evacuate it from an area of impending danger
Production flight tests and customer demonstration flights of new production aircraft
Fly over maximum takeoff weight on flights beyond normal range where landing places or fuel are lacking; the extra weight is limited to added fuel, fuel tanks and navigation equipment

body.p: How to get one:

bullets: Get help and forms from the local FSDO or a Designated Airworthiness Representative (DAR) [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].
An FAA inspector may inspect the aircraft or require an A&P or repair station to inspect it; the inspection is recorded in the aircraft records [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

Apply under 14 CFR 21.199 [[60:126|14 CFR 39.25]] with a statement giving: the purpose of the flight, the proposed itinerary, the crew needed, how the aircraft does not meet airworthiness requirements, any restrictions you consider needed for safety, and anything else the FAA asks for [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(a)]].

The FAA may inspect or test the aircraft, or require you to [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(b)]]. For an AD, the FAA may add requirements or decline if the aircraft cannot be moved safely [[60:126|14 CFR 39.23]].

callout.text: Overdue annual? A special flight permit can get you to the inspection, but all ADs that are due must be done before the flight [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Broken equipment that cannot be deferred can also be flown under a permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

check.q: Your annual expired while the plane sat at a field with no mechanic. What do you need to fly it to a shop?
check.a: A special flight permit from the FAA (FSDO), with all due ADs complied with first [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

chunks.title: Preventive maintenance a pilot can do

body.p: Preventive maintenance is simple or minor preservation and replacing small standard parts, with no complex assembly. Only items on the 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c) list count [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

head: Who
Rule
rows: A Part 61 pilot certificate holder (not sport) may do it on an aircraft he or she owns or operates, not used under Parts 121, 129 or 135
At least a private pilot may approve the aircraft for return to service afterward

Student and recreational pilots may do the work but cannot approve return to service (that needs at least a private pilot). Sport pilots: only on an LSA they own or operate. (PHAK 9-12 says student and recreational pilots are excluded; the current regulation allows the work.)

body.p: Common examples from Appendix A(c) [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)]] [[60:143|App. A(c)(21)-(31)]]:

bullets: Remove, install and repair landing gear tires; service shock struts with oil or air; clean and grease wheel bearings
Replace defective safety wire or cotter keys; lubrication without disassembly
Replace safety belts; replace side windows (no structure involved)
Replace bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights
Replace or clean spark plugs and set the gap
Replace any cowling that does not need prop removal or flight control disconnection
Clean or replace fuel and oil strainers or filter elements; replace and service batteries

body.p: Do the work with the manufacturer's methods, and leave it at least as good as original [[60:135|14 CFR 43.13]]. Then make a logbook entry [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]:

bullets: Description of the work
Date completed
Your signature, certificate number and kind of certificate (this signature approves return to service for that work only)

callout.text: Section 8 of the AFM/POH (Handling, Service and Maintenance) also describes preventive maintenance pilots may do [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]].

check.q: You are a private pilot and rent a club airplane. You replace a burned-out landing light bulb. What must you do before flight?
check.a: Make a logbook entry with a description, the date, and your signature, certificate number and kind of certificate [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Bulb replacement is preventive maintenance [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(17)]].

chunks.title: Required equipment for day and night VFR

body.p: For airplanes with a standard airworthiness certificate, these items must be installed AND working [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]].

head: Day VFR (91.205(b))
Night VFR adds (91.205(c))
rows: Airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator
Approved position lights
Tachometer for each engine; oil pressure gauge (pressure system); oil temperature gauge (air-cooled); temperature gauge (liquid-cooled); manifold pressure gauge (altitude engine)
Approved aviation red or white anticollision light system
Fuel gauge for each tank; landing gear position indicator (if retractable)
One electric landing light, if operated for hire
Anticollision lights (small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996)
Adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment
Safety belt for each occupant 2 years or older; shoulder harnesses (front seats if made after July 18, 1978; all seats after December 12, 1986)
One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind, accessible in flight
ELT if required by 91.207; flotation gear and a pyrotechnic signal if for hire over water beyond gliding distance from shore

callout.text: Study aids built from 91.205: Day = A TOMATO FLAMES (Airspeed, Tachometer, Oil pressure, Manifold pressure, Altimeter, Temperature (liquid-cooled), Oil temperature, Fuel gauges, Landing gear position, Anticollision lights, Magnetic compass, ELT, Safety belts/shoulder harnesses). Night adds FLAPS (Fuses, Landing light if for hire, Anticollision lights, Position lights, Source of electricity).

bullets: If an anticollision light fails, you may continue to a place where it can be repaired [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11), (c)(3)]].
Position lights must be on from sunset to sunrise; anticollision lights on whenever installed, unless the PIC turns them off for safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].

ELT exceptions include training flights entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport, and an ELT removed for repair for up to 90 days with a logbook entry and an 'ELT not installed' placard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

body.p: 91.205 is only the minimum. The AFM/POH equipment list shows what that airplane needs to be airworthy [[24:25|AFH 1-4]].

check.q: You are flying a friend at night, not for hire, and the landing light is out. Is that legal under 91.205?
check.a: Yes. A landing light is required at night only if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]. Still, check the equipment list/KOEL and think about the risk.

body.p: Rule of thumb: all installed instruments and equipment must work before each departure [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. You may not take off with something inoperative unless you use an approved MEL or the 91.213(d) rule [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. Most training airplanes (non-turbine, small) use 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]].
Step 1. Is the broken item required by any of these? If YES to any, you cannot defer it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: The VFR-day type certification equipment for that airplane
The aircraft's equipment list, or the Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL) for the flight you plan
14 CFR 91.205 or another Part 91 rule for that kind of flight
An Airworthiness Directive
Remove it (cockpit control placarded, entry made per 43.9), OR deactivate it and placard it 'Inoperative'. If deactivating needs maintenance, it must be done and recorded under Part 43.
A certificated, appropriately rated pilot (or mechanic) decides the item is not a hazard to the aircraft.

callout.text: Removal always counts as maintenance, so a mechanic must do it. PHAK says deactivating can be as simple as pulling a circuit breaker [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. AC 91-67A is stricter: turning off a switch does not remove power, deactivation is not preventive maintenance, and an authorized person must do it and make the 43.9 logbook entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Follow your school's or owner's procedure.

bullets: Put the INOPERATIVE placard near the switch, control or indicator [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
When an inspector finds deferrable items, he or she placards each one 'Inoperative' and adds it to the signed, dated discrepancy list given to the owner [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].
The owner must have deferred items repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].
Deferrals are for problems found before flight, not in flight. In flight, use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

body.p: More from AC 91-67A, the FAA's guide to 91.213:

bullets: No application or FAA approval is needed to fly under 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]].
Equipment the KOEL requires for a kind of operation (VFR, IFR, day or night) may not be deferred for that operation [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].
The placard should be legible, near the control or indicator, and not cover other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].
Before flying, weigh weather, night, the airports, the route, diversion options, extra workload and fatigue with the item inoperative [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].

callout.text: Your choices when you find a broken item: cancel, get it fixed before flight, or defer it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

check.q: Before a day flight, the left position light is out. 91.205 day does not require it, the equipment list and KOEL do not require it for day VFR, and no AD covers it. What do you do?
check.a: Have it deactivated, placard it 'Inoperative', and decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Under AC 91-67A, an authorized person does the deactivation and logs it [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

body.p: There are three ways to fly with inoperative equipment: an MEL with an LOA, the 91.213(d) rule, or a special flight permit under 21.197 and 21.199 [[58:20|AC 91-67A 3.2]].
To fly with inoperative items under an MEL, all of these must be true [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]:

bullets: An approved MEL exists for that aircraft
A Letter of Authorization (LOA) from the Flight Standards office is in the aircraft (MEL + LOA = a supplemental type certificate)
The aircraft records available to the pilot have an entry describing the inoperative items
You follow all conditions and limits in the MEL and LOA

body.p: How an operator gets one: on written request, the FSDO issues the make/model Master MEL (MMEL), an LOA and the preamble. The operator writes operations and maintenance (O&M) procedures. The MMEL plus those procedures becomes the operator's MEL. The MEL, LOA, preamble and procedures document must be on board for each flight [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

bullets: Once an LOA is issued, using the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
An MEL may not include items required by the type certification rules and essential for safety, items an AD requires, or items Part 91 requires for that operation [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)]].
If a failed item is not listed as deferrable (examples: tachometer, flaps, stall warning device), repair it before departure or get a special flight permit [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: Your airplane has an MEL and LOA. Can you skip the MEL and use 91.213(d) instead because it is simpler?
check.a: No. Once an LOA is issued, MEL use is mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

chunks.title: Risk: broken equipment found before flight

body.p: Legal is not the same as safe. Inoperative equipment is an Aircraft ('A' in PAVE) hazard. An inoperative landing light can make a night flight more hazardous, even though Part 91 does not require one when not for hire [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

bullets: Ask: how does this item matter for the weather, time of day and route I expect? [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]
Redundancy: one radio may be fine for day VFR, but a failure matters more at night or in IMC [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].
Do not defer lightly, especially if other items are already inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
If the flight plan changes (night, clouds, longer trip), re-check: an item you could defer for day VFR may be required for night [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]].

callout.text: Good habit: look at the airworthiness status before the walk-around, then decide cancel / fix / defer. Write down what you decided and why.

check.q: Two items are out: one position light (defer for day) and the fuel gauge for the left tank. Can you defer both?
check.a: No. A fuel gauge for each tank is required for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(9)]], so it must be fixed first (or a special flight permit obtained).

body.p: Expect the examiner to hand you the logbooks and a scenario. Work in this order:

bullets: Point to the airworthiness certificate (displayed at the entrance) and the registration; say how long each is valid [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].
Find the last annual and say the last legal day; check 100-hour if the flight is for hire [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]].
Find ELT inspection and battery date, transponder test (24 months), and altimeter/static test if IFR [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].
Show the AD compliance record and any recurring AD next due [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].
Open the POH: limitations, equipment list/KOEL, weight and balance [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
For a broken item, say out loud the 91.213(d) steps or the MEL steps, and your decision.

check.q: What document shows what equipment that specific airplane needs beyond 91.205?
check.a: The equipment list in the AFM/POH [[24:25|AFH 1-4]].

scenario.title: The evening cross-country
scenario.setup: Today is October 13. You are a new private pilot renting a club Cessna 172 (non-turbine, no MEL) for a trip to see family. You plan to leave at 3 p.m. and fly home after sunset. The logbook shows the annual signed off October 2 last year. During preflight you find the left wing position light will not light, and the landing light flickers.

questions.a: Yes. An annual signed off October 2 last year is good through October 31 this year (12 calendar months end on the last day of the month) [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

questions.q: Can you legally fly the daylight leg with the position light out?
questions.a: Possibly. Position lights are not on the 91.205 day list [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. If the equipment list/KOEL does not require them for day VFR and no AD applies, have the light deactivated, placard it 'Inoperative' and decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. Under AC 91-67A, an authorized person does the deactivation and makes the 43.9 logbook entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

questions.q: Can you fly home after sunset?
questions.a: No. Position lights are required for night VFR and must be on from sunset to sunrise [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. Fix it first or land before sunset.

questions.q: Can you replace the bulb yourself?
questions.a: Yes, if the club allows it. Replacing position light bulbs is preventive maintenance [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(17)]], a private pilot may do it on an aircraft he or she operates [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] and approve return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. Log it per 43.9 [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. A student pilot could do the work [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] but could not approve the airplane for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]].

questions.q: The landing light is not required for a flight not for hire. Should it change your plan?
questions.a: Think about risk, not only the rule. An inoperative landing light is an 'A' hazard that makes night operations more hazardous [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Get it fixed or plan a daylight return.

skills.do: Find the airworthiness and registration certificates in the airplane, explain where each must be, and how long each is valid. Point out the operating limitations, weight and balance data and data plate.
skills.practice: On your next preflight, find every document on the AFH 2-4 list in your training airplane and say why each is there.

skills.do: Using the logbooks and the examiner's scenario, show the annual (and 100-hour if needed), ELT, transponder and AD status, and decide if the airplane is airworthy.
skills.practice: Ask your CFI or the school for the logbooks. Fill out a one-page airworthiness summary like AFH Figure 2-4 with real due dates.

skills.do: Given a broken item, decide whether it can be deferred under 91.213(d) or the MEL, say how to deactivate and placard it, or decide to fix it or get a special flight permit.
skills.practice: Have your CFI name random broken items (position light, fuel gauge, landing light, tachometer) for day and night flights and talk through 91.205 and 91.213(d) for each.

quiz.q: An annual inspection was completed on June 14, 2026. What is the last day the airplane may fly without a new annual?
quiz.why: 12 calendar months runs to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

quiz.q: A 100-hour inspection comes due away from home. How far may you exceed it to reach an inspection shop?
quiz.why: Not more than 10 hours, and the extra time counts toward the next 100 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

quiz.q: Where must the airworthiness certificate be?
options: Displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance, readable by passengers or crew
In the glovebox, anywhere in the aircraft

quiz.q: Which of these can a private pilot owner do as preventive maintenance?
options: Replace a cowling that requires removing the propeller
quiz.why: Replacing bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights is on the Appendix A(c) list [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(17)]]. Transponders are excluded from avionics swaps [[60:143|App. A(c)(31)]].

quiz.q: For night VFR not for hire, which item is NOT required by 91.205?
quiz.why: A landing light is required only if operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].

quiz.q: Without an MEL, what must you do to a deferrable inoperative item before takeoff?
options: Have it removed or deactivated, and placard it 'Inoperative'
Get a special flight permit every time
quiz.why: Removal needs a placarded control and a 43.9 entry; deactivation needs an 'Inoperative' placard, and any maintenance must be done and recorded under Part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]]. AC 91-67A says an authorized person must do the deactivation and make the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

quiz.q: Who is primarily responsible for keeping an aircraft airworthy, including AD compliance?
options: The last mechanic who worked on it

quiz.q: An ELT battery must be replaced when it has been used for more than ___ or when ___ of its useful life has expired.
How often must the transponder be tested and inspected?

options: One that requires compliance before further flight
One due at the next annual
One that applies only to airliners
quiz.why: Emergency ADs require immediate compliance prior to further flight [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

quiz.q: An aircraft registration certificate was issued on March 10, 2026. When does it expire?
options: Never, unless the aircraft is sold
quiz.why: A registration certificate expires seven years after the last day of the month in which it was issued [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]].

takeaways: The owner keeps the airplane airworthy; the PIC decides if it is safe to fly today [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]] [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403]].
Airworthiness certificate displayed at the entrance, registration on board [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203]].
Annual within 12 calendar months; 100-hour if for hire; ELT 12 months; transponder 24 months [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]].
ADs are law; know their status and recurring due times [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7]].
Broken item: required by type cert, equipment list/KOEL, 91.205 or AD? Then fix it. If not, deactivate/remove, placard and decide no hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].
Legal is not always safe: weigh each broken item against your planned flight [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].
cfi_notes: Students mix up 'calendar months' with exact dates. Have them compute due dates from real logbook entries.
Common error: thinking 91.205 is the whole story. Make them check the POH equipment list and KOEL too (91.213(d)(2)).
Students often think they can remove a broken item themselves. Removal is maintenance; a pilot may only deactivate when no maintenance is needed (PHAK 9-9/9-10).
Examiners like changing the scenario mid-question: day to night, not for hire to for hire, VFR to IFR. Drill these switches.

Preventive maintenance: 43.3(g) lets pilot certificate holders do it, but 43.7(f) requires at least a private pilot to approve return to service. Student and recreational pilots may do the work but cannot sign it off. PHAK 9-12 says they are excluded entirely; teach the regulation.
Use the school's real logbooks for S2 practice; build an airworthiness summary sheet like AFH Figure 2-4.
The MEL figure is a helicopter MMEL sample (the only one in these resources). Point out the columns, not the helicopter items.
Registration lasts seven years after the last day of the issue month (47.40, eCFR as of 10/09/2026). Older materials may show a shorter period; teach the current rule.

Pink copy: PHAK 9-7 says not more than 90 days. Current 47.31(c) has no day limit: valid inside the U.S. until the certificate arrives or the application is denied, and not usable once 12 months have passed since the first application after a transfer. Teach the regulation.

Deactivation: PHAK 9-9/9-10 suggests a pilot may pull a breaker; AC 91-67A 4.2.2 says deactivation is not preventive maintenance and an authorized person must do it and log it. Ask the school/owner which procedure they use.
gaps: Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins (SAIBs) are not described in any of the provided resources, including the newly added AC 91-67A and 14 CFR Parts 21 and 47 (K1c).
KOEL content and location are POH-specific. AC 91-67A 1.8.9 explains what a KOEL is and that it has no standard format, but no sample KOEL is in the resources.
ARROW and A TOMATO FLAMES / FLAPS are study aids built from the sourced lists; the acronyms themselves are not in the FAA resources.
PHAK 9-10 refers to AC 91-67, which AC 91-67A 1.4 says was canceled on November 3, 2017 [[58:6|AC 91-67A 1.4]]; the lesson uses AC 91-67A.

activities.title: Match the paper to its rule
activities.intro: Tap a document, then the rule that goes with it.

pairs.r: Displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance
Expires 7 years after the end of its issue month
Temporary authority, for flights inside the U.S. only
Needed for flights outside the U.S.
Normally not kept in the airplane

activities.title: How often is it due?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Altimeter and static system test, for IFR
Extra inspection when carrying passengers for hire
Extra inspection when a CFI gives paid lessons in a plane the CFI provides

activities.title: True or false: ADs, permits and pilot maintenance

cards.s: An AD needs an inspection every 50 hours. Like a 100-hour inspection, you may go up to 10 hours over to reach a shop.
cards.why: No. The 10-hour allowance is only for the 100-hour inspection [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. There is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD itself says so [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

cards.s: An AD still applies to a part even if that part was modified in the area the AD covers.
cards.why: Yes. An AD applies to each product it names, even if it was changed in that area [[60:125|14 CFR 39.15]].

cards.s: A special flight permit can be issued to move an airplane out of the path of a coming hurricane.
cards.why: Yes. Evacuating aircraft from areas of impending danger is one of the listed purposes [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)(4)]].

cards.s: A special flight permit lets you fly an unairworthy airplane on any trip you like, once it has been inspected.
cards.why: No. The permit is for a specific flight, such as flying to a base where repairs can be done, delivering the airplane, or leaving an area of danger [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

cards.s: A private pilot may clean the spark plugs on an airplane he or she owns, then approve it for return to service.
cards.why: Yes. Cleaning spark plugs is preventive maintenance [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(20)]], and at least a private pilot may approve return to service after it [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]].

cards.s: Replacing a cowling that requires removing the propeller is preventive maintenance.
cards.why: No. Only a cowling that does not need prop removal or disconnecting flight controls is on the list [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(19)]].

activities.title: Defer a broken item, no MEL
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Find the broken item during preflight, before departure
Confirm it is not required by type certification, equipment list/KOEL, 91.205 or an AD
Have it removed or deactivated, with any maintenance logged
Placard it 'Inoperative' near its switch or indicator
After the flight, have it fixed or inspected at the next required inspection

final_quiz.q: You rent a club airplane, and the club takes care of its maintenance. During the climb you find an unairworthy structural problem. What does the rule require of you?
options: Keep flying, since the owner is responsible for airworthiness
Finish the planned trip, then report it to the club
Call the club by radio and ask if you may continue
final_quiz.why: The PIC must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The owner's duty to maintain the airplane does not remove this [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Today is October 16, 2026. Which annual inspection sign-off date makes the airplane overdue today?
final_quiz.why: 12 calendar months run to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. A September 30, 2025 annual ran out on September 30, 2026. An October 2025 annual is good through October 31, 2026 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A school airplane used for paid instruction had its last 100-hour inspection at 2,400.0 hours. It flew to a shop and was inspected at 2,506.0 hours. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
final_quiz.why: You may go up to 10 hours over to reach a shop, but the extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. It was due at 2,500.0, so the next one is due at 2,600.0, not at 2,506.0 + 100.

final_quiz.q: During preflight you find the registration certificate, but the airworthiness certificate is nowhere in the cabin. What is correct?
options: You may fly, because the FAA keeps a copy on file
You may fly if the logbooks are on board
You may fly day VFR only
You may not fly until it is displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance
final_quiz.why: No one may operate a civil aircraft unless the airworthiness certificate is displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's registration certificate expires on June 30, 2027. When may you send in the renewal application (AC Form 8050-1B) and fee?
options: During the six months before June 30, 2027
Only in the 30 days before June 30, 2027
Each year on the date it was issued
final_quiz.why: Renewal is filed with AC Form 8050-1B and the fee during the six months before the expiration date [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(b)]].

final_quiz.q: A friend offers you a ride in his experimental airplane. Unless the FAA has authorized otherwise, which limit applies?
options: It may fly VFR, day only
It may not carry any passengers
It needs a new annual before every flight
Only a commercial pilot may fly it
final_quiz.why: An experimental aircraft is operated VFR, day only, unless specifically authorized. The pilot must also tell each person carried that it is experimental [[60:511|14 CFR 91.319(d)]].

final_quiz.q: An AD on your engine is based on the engine maker's service bulletin, but the two give different instructions. Which do you follow?
options: The service bulletin, since the maker knows the engine best
Either one, as the mechanic chooses
final_quiz.why: If the service document and the AD conflict, you must follow the AD [[60:126|14 CFR 39.27]]. ADs are legally enforceable rules [[60:125|14 CFR 39.3]].

final_quiz.q: You are checking the logbooks. An AD on the propeller needs a repeat inspection. What must the AD status record show for it?
options: Only the date it was first complied with
The pilot's signature after each flight
The service bulletin number in place of the AD number
The method of compliance and the time and date the next action is due
final_quiz.why: The AD status record shows the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and, for recurring action, the time and date the next action is required [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's annual ran out while it sat at a field with no mechanic. You apply for a special flight permit to fly it to a shop. What must your application state?
options: The ways the airplane does not meet airworthiness requirements
Proof that you hold a commercial pilot certificate
A signed release from your insurance company
final_quiz.why: The statement must give the purpose, the itinerary, the crew needed, the ways the aircraft does not meet airworthiness requirements, any restrictions needed for safety, and anything else the FAA asks for [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You are a private pilot and own your airplane. A main tire is worn, so you remove it and install a new one yourself. What is true?
options: Only an A&P mechanic may change a tire, so you need to hire one
You may do it, but a mechanic must approve the airplane for return to service
You may do it and approve the airplane for return to service yourself, with a logbook entry
Changing a tire is a major repair that needs FAA Form 337
final_quiz.why: Removing, installing and repairing landing gear tires is preventive maintenance [[60:142|Part 43 App. A(c)(1)]]. A Part 61 pilot (not a sport pilot) may do preventive maintenance on an airplane he or she owns [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]], and a private pilot or higher may approve it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. You must record the work in the maintenance records [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9]].

final_quiz.q: Before a day VFR flight in a small airplane with an air-cooled engine and no MEL, you find a broken item. Which one can never be deferred under 91.213(d) for this flight?
options: The landing light, on a flight not for hire
final_quiz.why: An oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine is required for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(7)]]. Items required by 91.205 may not be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. The others are not on the day list.

final_quiz.q: Your small airplane has an approved MEL and a Letter of Authorization. The stall warning device fails, and it is not listed in the MEL as deferrable. No shop is at this airport. What are your choices?
options: Defer it under 91.213(d), since that is simpler
Placard it and fly, because it is day VFR
Repair it before departure, or get a special flight permit to fly to a shop
Fly, because the stall warning is not on the 91.205 list
final_quiz.why: If a failed item is not listed in the MEL as deferrable, repairs are required before departure, or a special flight permit can be obtained to fly to a shop [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Once an LOA is issued, the MEL must be used [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: You start a day flight with an inoperative position light properly deferred. A weather delay means you would now land 30 minutes after sunset. What is the best choice?
options: Continue, because the deferral covers the whole flight
Land before sunset, or have the light fixed before flying at night
Continue, as long as the anticollision lights work
Continue, as long as you tell ATC about the light
final_quiz.why: Position lights are required for night VFR and must be lit from sunset to sunrise [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. Always weigh a broken item against the flight conditions you now expect [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].
